tldr: A human stand-up motion recorded on hard ground was adapted to a humanoid robot standing up stably on soft ground with up to ~40 mm of surface penetration, using a two-stage reinforcement learning framework with tuned MuJoCo contact parameters.
hero_caption: Simulation snapshots of the Unitree G1 standing up from a fallen state on deformable ground. While preserving the human demonstration pattern, the robot adapts to the delayed support force generation caused by surface penetration and recovers to a stable upright posture.
overview:
For humanoid robots to operate autonomously in outdoor and unstructured environments, the ability to stand up after falling is essential. However, on soft, deformable terrain such as grass or foam mats, the ground sinks significantly under the robot's weight to generate support forces, which severely disrupts posture and balance. At the same time, collecting stand-up demonstration data on soft ground from robots or humans is difficult.

To address this, the authors proposed a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework that takes human motion capture stand-up data recorded on hard ground and adapts it to deformable ground in simulation. Deformable terrain is emulated using parameters (solref and solimp) from MuJoCo's rigid-body soft-contact model. The policy is first trained to imitate the demonstration on hard ground, and then fine-tuned after the ground is made softer. Crucially, the reward design does not merely track demonstration joint angles; it also explicitly evaluates recovery objectives such as pelvis height, torso uprightness, and the final standing posture.

In simulation experiments with the 29-DOF Unitree G1 humanoid, the policy successfully recovered to the target upright posture while preserving the whole-body coordination of the demonstration, even on soft surfaces where penetration reached approximately 40 mm. Furthermore, ablation experiments revealed that tracking the demonstration joint trajectories alone fails on soft ground, showing that explicit recovery rewards for posture and height are indispensable.
contributions: Proposed a two-stage reinforcement learning framework that adapts human demonstration data collected on hard ground to deformable terrain where surface penetration occurs.
Reused MuJoCo contact parameters (solref and solimp) to efficiently emulate deformable ground with surface penetration and delayed support forces while maintaining flat surface geometry.

Achieved stand-up on soft terrain with up to ~40 mm of penetration by combining reference tracking via residual joint-position control with progressive recovery rewards evaluating pelvis height and torso uprightness.
Experimentally demonstrated that reference tracking alone is insufficient for standing up on soft ground, and that combining it with global posture recovery rewards is essential.

sections.heading: Why is standing up on soft ground so hard?
sections.summary: The ability to stand up is vital for humanoid autonomy in outdoor settings, but surface penetration on deformable ground poses a major balance challenge. This study proposes adapting hard-ground human demonstrations to soft ground using a two-stage learning method.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to operate over extended periods in diverse environments such as factories and outdoors, robust stand-up behavior is required so they can recover on their own after falling. Unlike steady walking, standing up is a non-periodic task where multiple body parts make intermittent contact with the ground. Furthermore, on deformable soft terrain like grass or cushions, significant surface penetration occurs before sufficient reaction force is generated to support the robot's body weight, drastically altering the robot's posture and center of pressure (CoP: the point within the support polygon where the ground reaction force acts).

Previous approaches for generating stand-up motions have explored predefined sequence playback, optimization-based methods such as model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning (RL), and imitation learning tracking motion capture data. However, most existing RL stand-up methods assume hard ground. Even when terrain compliance was considered, it was typically limited to slight variations as a domain randomization parameter. As a result, the effects of large deformations, delayed support forces, and changing contact geometry on stand-up motions have remained largely unaddressed.

To tackle this, this study uses easily obtainable human stand-up demonstrations on hard ground as a reference and develops a two-stage RL framework to adapt the 29-DOF Unitree G1 humanoid to deformable terrain. By adjusting MuJoCo's contact dynamics parameters, the approach generates stand-up motions that overcome both the large penetration and delayed force buildup unique to soft surfaces, all while preserving the smooth whole-body coordination of the demonstration.

sections.heading: Hacking MuJoCo's contact model with two-stage residual learning
sections.summary: Deformable ground penetration is emulated using MuJoCo's contact constraint parameters and learned via PPO with residual joint-position control. After initial training on rigid ground, the surface is softened, and stable stand-up is acquired through a reset noise curriculum and phased reward transitions.
sections.details:
The proposed method uses reference trajectories retargeted to the Unitree G1 humanoid (recalculating joint trajectories to fit the robot's kinematic structure) from stand-up motions in the public BONES-SEED dataset. The policy operates at 60 Hz and outputs residual joint positions $\mathbf{a}_t$ that correct deviations from the 120 Hz reference trajectory. The commanded joint angles are computed as $\mathbf{q}^\mathrm{cmd}_t = \mathbf{q}^\mathrm{ref}_t + s_a \mathbf{a}_t$ (action scaler $s_a = 0.25$) and converted into torques via joint-level PD controllers. The policy observation includes current joint states, errors relative to the reference state, differences from the target standing posture, the normalized motion phase $\phi_t \in [0, 1]$, and the previous action.

To emulate soft terrain, the framework leverages the parameters `solref` (reference stiffness $\kappa$ and damping $c$) and `solimp` (constraint impedance function $\gamma$) from MuJoCo's rigid-body contact model. Starting from the default hard ground settings, these are changed to critically damped behavior with a time constant of 0.1 s, with impedance smoothly ramping from 0 to 0.95 over a penetration depth of 0.02 m (20 mm). This reproduces penetration behavior and delayed force generation—comparable to loading a ~5 cm thick urethane foam—without requiring geometric mesh deformation.

Training follows a two-stage curriculum. First, roughly 70 million PPO steps are trained in the hard ground environment. The reward combines trajectory tracking terms (joint positions, velocities, torso, and foot positions) with recovery completion terms (pelvis height, torso uprightness, and final standing posture), smoothly shifting weight from tracking to recovery as the phase $\phi_t$ advances. Next, the ground parameters are switched to the soft setting, the learning rate is reduced from $3 \times 10^{-4}$ to $1 \times 10^{-4}$, and fine-tuning is performed for another 20 million steps. During this soft-ground phase, a reset noise curriculum gradually expands Gaussian noise added to initial joint angles and velocities, improving robustness against variations in initial surface penetration.

sections.heading: Surviving 40 mm of sinking: What the ablations revealed
sections.summary: The policy succeeded in standing up on both hard and soft surfaces across two distinct stand-up sequences. Maximum penetration reached approximately 40 mm, and ablation results confirmed that explicit global posture recovery rewards are essential, as reference tracking alone fails.
sections.details:
The trained policy successfully recovered to the target upright posture on both hard and soft ground across two demonstration trajectories featuring different initial postures and motion sequences. As shown in the snapshots of Fig. F2, the robot maintains natural human-like stand-up coordination while automatically applying subtle joint adjustments to maintain balance during phases where contact loads are concentrated.

Quantitative evaluation measuring pelvis height and torso uprightness (the inner product of the torso's local vertical axis and the world vertical axis) showed that the robot reached 0.792 m against a target pelvis height of 0.794 m, and achieved an uprightness of 0.991, indicating a virtually complete vertical posture (Fig. F1). Contact analysis (Fig. F3) confirmed the transition from initial whole-body contact to final dual-foot support, with a maximum contact penetration depth reaching $\delta_{\max} = 39.4$ mm into the surface. The controller proved capable of withstanding the demanding conditions unique to soft terrain, where pushing against the ground causes immediate sinking and delayed reaction forces.

Crucial insights were gained from ablation experiments. Comparing training with reference tracking rewards alone versus the full proposed reward design showed that the root-mean-square (RMS) tracking error across all 29 joints was nearly identical at approximately 0.156–0.157 rad in both cases. However, the tracking-only policy only reached a maximum pelvis height of 0.130 m, and uprightness collapsed to 0.543, resulting in complete stand-up failure. In other words, on soft ground, perfectly tracing the demonstration joint angles is not enough to compensate for center-of-mass shifts caused by penetration; global recovery rewards that directly encourage pelvis height and uprightness are indispensable.

captions.F1: Evolution of pelvis height (red curve) and torso uprightness (yellow curve) during the stand-up motion. During the lifting phase (phase > 0.65), pelvis height rapidly rises toward the target value (~0.79 m), and uprightness reaches nearly 1.0 (fully upright).
captions.F3: Evolution of maximum penetration depth (top) and the number of active contact points (bottom) during the motion. A maximum penetration of approximately 40 mm occurs during the pushing phase, and contact points transition from whole-body contacts to sole contacts only.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next
sections.summary: This work demonstrated that a humanoid can learn to stand up on soft ground using hard-ground demonstrations via two-stage reinforcement learning. Future directions include modeling lateral resistance forces and testing on physical hardware.
sections.details:
This study presented a method for adapting human stand-up demonstrations recorded on rigid ground to deformable terrain using residual reinforcement learning and MuJoCo contact dynamics. By adopting a two-stage approach—pre-training on hard ground followed by adaptation to soft terrain—the policy successfully acquired stand-up behaviors that overcome up to ~40 mm of penetration while preserving the natural motion patterns of the demonstration.

The findings show that even when high-quality demonstrations can only be captured on hard floors, transfer to compliant terrain is possible with suitable simulation modeling and reward design. The code has been open-sourced to ensure reproducibility, serving as a stepping stone for future legged robot control on unstructured terrain.

takeaways: On soft ground, merely matching joint angles is not enough; explicitly incorporating task objectives like pelvis height and torso uprightness into the reward is essential.
Tuning MuJoCo's rigid-body soft-contact parameters (solref, solimp) allows lightweight emulation of penetration on the order of tens of millimeters without complex finite element modeling.
A two-stage curriculum that pre-trains core coordination on hard ground before transitioning to soft ground is effective for balancing natural motion retention with environmental adaptation.
limitations: All validations were conducted entirely in simulation; experimental validation on physical humanoid hardware (Unitree G1) was not performed.
Due to constraints in MuJoCo's contact model, only penetration along the surface normal is emulated, leaving out tangential (lateral) deformation and dragging resistance when feet are submerged.

Robustness handled by the reset noise curriculum was limited to small variations in initial joint angles and velocities, without covering lateral push disturbances or friction coefficient randomization.
